rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about the city’s hypocrites may continue the preceding subject, making ‘mardū’ an independent predicate that says they are deeply practiced in hypocrisy.
rows.anchor: ويكون مردوا استئنافا، أخبر عنهم أنهم خريجون في النفاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He finds it awkward to make ‘mardū’ an adjective of ‘hypocrites’ because a coordinated phrase separates adjective and noun.
rows.anchor: ويبعد أن يكون مردوا صفة للمبتدأ الذي هو منافقون

rows.speaker: الزمخشري والزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī, following al-Zajjāj, allows ‘mardū’ to modify the distant subject ‘hypocrites.’
rows.anchor: وقد أجازه الزمخشري تابعا للزجاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another parse treats the phrase as a new clause with an omitted subject such as ‘people’ or ‘hypocrites’ from Medina.
rows.anchor: ويقدر موصوف محذوف هو المبتدأ أي: ومن أهل المدينة قوم مردوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says the analogy ‘I am the son of Jala’ works only for generic omission; its specific form is awkward because that construction is poetic necessity.
rows.anchor: وأما أن ابن جلا فضرورة شعر كقوله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains ‘mardū’ as becoming practiced and firmly established in hypocrisy.
rows.anchor: وقال هنا ابن عباس: مردوا، مرنوا وثبتوا

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda glosses ‘mardū’ as being rebellious or obstinate, from tamarrada.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: عتوا من قولهم تمرد

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says they persisted in hypocrisy and did not repent.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: أقاموا عليه لم يتوبوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘You do not know them’ may mean that the Prophet would know them only when God made them known, or did not know their outcome, or could not know their inward hypocrisy.
rows.anchor: لا تعلمهم أي: حتى نعلمك بهم، أو لا تعلم عواقب أمرهم

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmānī takes ‘you do not know them’ as ‘you do not know them as hypocrites’; the earlier mention of hypocrites supplies an omitted object.
rows.anchor: فدل على المحذوف، فتعدت إلى اثنين قاله: الكرماني

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says their extreme caution conceals them despite the Prophet’s insight and sound discernment.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: يخفون عليك مع فطنتك وشهامتك وصدق فراستك

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda warns against pretending to know whether particular people are destined for Paradise or Hell, since even people know their own deeds imperfectly.
rows.anchor: قال: فما بال أقوام يتكلفون علم الناس؟ فلان في الجنة، فلان في النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān condemns later self-styled mystics for unsupported claims about the unseen and says Qatāda’s warning remains apt.
rows.anchor: والتجري على الإخبار الكاذب عن المغيبات، لقضى من ذلك العجب

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains that God knows their hidden disbelief while they outwardly resemble sincere believers because they are highly practiced hypocrites.
rows.anchor: نطلع على سرهم، لأنهم يبطنون الكفر في سويداء قلوبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘We know them’ is a threat, followed by the warning that God will punish them twice.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله: نحن نعلمهم تهديد وترتب عليه بقوله: سنعذبهم مرتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dual punishment may literally mean two punishments, or figuratively mean repeated punishment, as ‘twice’ can mean one event after another.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون لا يراد بها شفع الواحد، بل يكون المعنى على التكثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most interpreters identify the second punishment as punishment in the grave.
rows.anchor: فأكثر الناس على أن العذاب الثاني هو عذاب القبر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās’s best-known view is that the first punishment was public exposure and branding as hypocrites.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس في الأشهر عنه: هو فضيحتهم ووصمهم بالنفاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet publicly named and expelled a group of hypocrites from the mosque during Friday prayer; ʿUmar initially mistook the departing people for the congregation leaving.
rows.anchor: اخرج يا فلان من المسجد فإنك منافق، واخرج أنت يا فلان

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya views the expulsions as disciplinary judgment that did not remove the men from Islam, comparable to expelling wrongdoers.
rows.anchor: وفعله صلى الله عليه وسلم على جهة التأديب اجتهاد منه فيهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects Ibn ʿAṭiyya’s comparison: explicitly calling each expelled man a hypocrite means the Prophet judged him an unbeliever, not merely a disobedient Muslim.
rows.anchor: ويبعد ما قال ابن عطية لأنه نص على نفاق من أخرج بعينه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: The report identifies al-dubayla as a flame of Hell that burns from a man’s shoulder to his chest.
rows.anchor: ستة منهم تكفيهم الدبيلة سراج من نار جهنم تأخذ في كتف أحدهم حتى تفضي إلى صدره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet privately told Ḥudhayfa that twelve hypocrites would die: six from a fiery boil and six by other deaths.
rows.anchor: وروي أنه أسر إلى حذيفة باثني عشر منهم وقال

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the punishments were killing and hunger; the source calls this unlikely because some were not affected by either.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: هو عذابهم بالقتل والجوع. قيل: وهذا بعيد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās identifies punishment as enforcing religious legal duties on them despite their dislike.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا: هو هو أنهم بإقامة حدود الشرع عليهم

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq says their punishment was distress at Islam’s public emergence and ascendancy.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن إسحاق: هو همهم بظهور الإسلام وعلو كلمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view is that angels strike their faces and backs when their souls are taken.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ضرب الملائكة وجوههم وأدبارهم عند قبض أرواحهم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says the first punishment is confiscation of their wealth and the second is forced jihad, which they regard as punishment.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: الأول ما يؤخذ من أموالهم قهرا

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd takes the two punishments as worldly afflictions through wealth and children, with each kind itself counted as repeated punishment.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: مرتين هما عذاب الدنيا بالأموال والأولاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other suggestions are the destruction of the Mosque of Harm and then Hellfire; all agree the great punishment is the afterlife punishment.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إحراق مسجد الضرار، والآخر إحراقهم بنار جهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anas’s codex reads ‘He will punish them’ with a yāʾ; ʿAyyāsh transmitted a vowelless yāʾ form from Abū ʿAmr.
rows.anchor: وفي مصحف أنس سيعذبهم بالياء، وسكن عياش عن أبي عمر والياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The confession verse is said to concern ten men who stayed behind from Tabūk; reports vary on whether ten, eight, seven, six, five, or three were involved and who bound themselves in the mosque.
rows.anchor: نزلت في عشرة رهط تخلفوا عن غزوة تبوك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One report names three who tied themselves to the mosque pillars: Abū Lubāba, Aws ibn Thaʿlaba, and Wadīʿa ibn Khidhām.
rows.anchor: ثلاثة أبو لبابة بن عبد المنذر، وأوس بن ثعلبة، ووديعة بن خذام الأنصاري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report that the verse concerned only Abū Lubāba is unlikely because the wording ‘others’ is plural.
rows.anchor: ويبعد ذلك من لفظ وآخرون، لأنه جمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the Prophet’s return, the bound men said they would remain tied until he released them; he also swore to wait for revelation, then released and excused them after the verse came down.
rows.anchor: رغبوا عني، وتخلفوا عن الغزو مع المسلمين» فنزلت

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the verse concerns Abū Lubāba’s advice to Banū Qurayẓa to surrender, signaling with his throat that the Prophet would execute them; he repented and bound himself to a mosque pillar until forgiven.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: نزلت في أبي لبابة في شأنه مع بني قريظة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The men’s confession is an admission of sin; the good deed is repentance and remorse, while the bad deed is their failure to join the expedition or, in another account, their earlier departure for jihad.
rows.anchor: والاعتراف: الإقرار بالذنب عملا صالحا توبة وندما، وآخر سيئا

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī takes the bad deed as staying behind from this expedition; al-Ḥasan and others also contrast prior jihad with this absence, while al-Kalbī says it means repentance mixed with sin.
rows.anchor: أي تخلفا عن هذه الغزاة قاله: الطبري، أو خروجا إلى الجهاد قبل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī argues that coordinating the two deeds makes each one both mixed and mixed-with, unlike saying water was mixed into milk, which marks only the water as mixed.
rows.anchor: وعطف أحدهما على الآخر دليل على أن كل واحد منهما مخلوط ومخلوط به

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī also compares the construction to ‘I sold the sheep, a sheep and a dirham,’ meaning a sheep for a dirham.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون من قولهم: بعت الشاء شاة ودرهما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says ‘perhaps’ is certain when spoken by God; Abū Ḥayyān says its tentative wording leaves believers in hope and apprehension before concluding with forgiveness and mercy.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: عسى من الله واجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although revealed about particular men, the verse applies generally to the Muslim community until the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية وإن نزلت في ناس. مخصوصين فهي عامة في الأمة إلى يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: أبو عثمان
rows.claim: Abū ʿUthmān considers this among the most hope-giving verses in the Qur’an for the community.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عثمان: ما في القرآن آية أرجى عندي لهذه الأمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Bayhaqī account of the Ascension shows repentant people who mixed good and bad deeds around Abraham, their colors cleansed by bathing in three rivers before rejoining white-faced companions.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث الإسراء والمعراج من تخريج البيهقي: أن الذين خلطوا عملا صالحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address is to the Prophet and its pronoun refers to the repentant latecomers; they offer their wealth and ask him to purify them, but he says he was not ordered to take it until this verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: الخطاب للرسول، والضمير عائد على الذين خلطوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet took one-third of their property in response to ‘take from their wealth.’
rows.anchor: فيروى أنه أخذ ثلث أموالهم مراعاة لقوله: خذ من أموالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most early interpreters place the verse among the repentant stragglers; a group of jurists instead reads it as the obligatory zakāt.
rows.anchor: والذي تظاهرت به أقوال المتأولين ابن عباس وغيره: أنها في هؤلاء المتخلفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the zakāt reading, ‘their wealth’ means zakatable assets generally, excluding houses and clothing, and no fixed amount is specified, so even a small voluntary amount can count.
rows.anchor: إذ يخرج عنه الأموال التي لا زكاة فيها كالرباع والثياب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command ‘take’ indicates that the imam is responsible for collecting and administering alms.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله: خذ، دليل على أن الإمام هو الذي يتولى أخذ الصدقات وينظر فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He parses ‘from their wealth’ with ‘take’; ‘purifying them’ can be a circumstantial clause whose subject is the implied subject of ‘take,’ among other parses.
rows.anchor: ومن أموالهم: متعلق بخذ وتطهرهم، وتزكيهم حال من ضمير خذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects making ‘purifying them’ modify charity while ‘you purify’ is a separate circumstance unless an implied subject is supplied; that construction is rare.
rows.anchor: وهذا فاسد المعنى، ولو كان بغير واو جاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Purification may mean intensified cleansing, or growth and blessing in wealth.
rows.anchor: والتزكية مبالغة في التطهر وزيادة فيه، أو بمعنى الإنماء والبركة في المال

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reads the verb in a causative form as another way to express purification.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن: تطهرهم من أطهر واطهر وطهر للتعدية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Pray for them’ may mean supplicate, ask forgiveness, or perform funeral prayer for them.
rows.anchor: وصل عليهم أي ادع لهم، أو استغفر لهم، أو صل عليهم إذا ماتوا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains the Prophet’s prayer as reassurance that God accepted their charity; he also reports meanings of mercy and nearness.
rows.anchor: قاله: ابن عباس. أو رحمة لهم قاله أيضا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the Prophet’s prayer gives them increased dignity.
rows.anchor: أو زيادة وقار لهم قاله: قتادة

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda understands ‘sakan’ as strengthening their hearts; other glosses include security.
rows.anchor: أو تثبيت لقلوبهم قاله: أبو عبيدة، أو أمن لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited poem uses ‘sakan’ in the sense of shelter or comfort; the several glosses are close in meaning.
rows.anchor: وهذه أقوال متقاربة

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī gives a philosophical account: the Prophet’s radiant soul affects the repentants’ souls through prayer, clarifying and elevating them.
rows.anchor: لأن روحه صلى الله عليه وسلم كانت روحا قوية مشرقة صافية

rows.speaker: ابن النقيب
rows.claim: Ibn al-Naqīb rejects al-Rāzī’s explanation as philosophical and incompatible with the method of Qur’anic exegesis.
rows.anchor: كلام الرازي كلام فلسفي يشير فيه إلى أن قوى الأنفس مؤثرة فعالة

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda say the repentants from whom charity was taken were distinct from the three whose case was deferred.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن وقتادة: في هؤلاء المعترفين المأخوذ منهم الصدقة هم سوى الثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Two canonical readers and Ḥafṣ read ‘your prayer’ in the singular here and at Hūd 11:87; the rest read the plural.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأخوان وحفص: إن صلاتك هنا، وفي هود صلاتك بالتوحيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God hears their confession and knows their remorse and repentance.
rows.anchor: والله سميع باعترافهم، عليم بندامتهم وتوبتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse was revealed after some who had not repented complained that the repentants had once been shunned and not spoken to.
rows.anchor: قال الذين لم يتوبوا من المتخلفين: هؤلاء كانوا بالأمس معنا لا يكلمون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ubayy’s codex and a reported reading of al-Ḥasan address the audience directly with ‘Do you not know?’ instead of ‘Do they not know?’
rows.anchor: وفي مصحف أبي وقراءة الحسن بخلاف عنه: ألم تعلموا بالتاء على الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source notes that ʿan and min can alternate within a single expression, as in describing charity as given from wealth.
rows.anchor: وعن بمعنى من، وكثيرا ما يتوصل في موضع واحد بهذه، وهذه تقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say ʿan and min are close in meaning, but ʿan adds a sense of distance.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كلمة من وكلمة عن متقاربتان، إلا أن عن تفيد البعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation says the wording teaches a penitent to feel distant from God’s acceptance because of the sin, producing humility before the Lord.
rows.anchor: فيفيدها أن التائب يجب أن يعتقد في نفسه أنه بعيد عن قبول الله توبته

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān explains that taking knowledge ‘from’ Zayd via ʿan denotes its transfer to the hearer, while min marks the starting point; ʿan expresses the transfer more clearly.
rows.anchor: فإن قلت: أخذت العلم عن زيد فمعناه أنه جاوز إليك، وإذا قلت: من زيد دل على ابتداء الغاية

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: When repentance passes from the servants toward God, He is described as turning toward them in acceptance.
rows.anchor: وكأنهم لما جاوزت توبتهم عنهم إلى الله، اتصف هو تعالى بالتوبة عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He explains ‘from’ in ‘accept repentance from His servants’ as indicating passage or transfer toward God, more pointedly than ‘from’ as a starting point.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر من موضوع عن أنها للمجاوزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reciprocal language of repentance is compared to the report that God approaches the servant more greatly than the servant approaches Him.
rows.anchor: ومن أتاني يمشي أتيته هرولة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Work’ is an imperative carrying a threat, and the apparent addressees are repentant men who had stayed behind.
rows.anchor: صيغة أمر ضمنها الوعيد، والمعتذرون التائبون من المتخلفين، هم المخاطبون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readings identify the addressees as unrepentant excuse-makers, or as both believers and hypocrites.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هم المعتذرون الذين لم يتوبوا. وقيل: المؤمنون والمنافقون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the address is to repentants, the wording deliberately echoes the warning to hypocrites and lowers their status, since they did not risk wealth and life alongside the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وأنهم وإن تابوا ليسوا كالذين جاهدوا معه بأموالهم وأنفسهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، وعكرمة، ومجاهد، والضحاك، وقتادة، وابن إسحاق
rows.claim: These authorities say the people whose case was deferred were the three who stayed behind before their repentance: Hilāl, Murāra, and Kaʿb.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس، وعكرمة، ومجاهد، والضحاك، وقتادة، وابن إسحاق: نزلت في الثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view makes them the hypocrites who delayed repentance while establishing the Mosque of Harm.
rows.anchor: وقيل: نزلت في المنافقين المعرضين للتوبة مع بنائهم مسجد الضرار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A group of named readers reads marjūn without hamza; the remaining canonical readers use hamza, and both are dialect forms.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن، وطلحة، وأبو جعفر، وابن نصاح، والأعرج، ونافع، وحمزة، والكسائي، وحفص: مرجون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘For God’s command’ means according to His wisdom: He may punish them if they persist or pardon them if they repent.
rows.anchor: لأمر الله أي الحكمة، إما يعذبهم إن أصروا ولم يتوبوا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says they were hypocrites whom the Prophet kept away from his presence.
rows.anchor: أرجأهم رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن حضرته

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: Al-Aṣamm says God delayed disclosing what He knew about the hypocrites and warned them to repent.
rows.anchor: وقال الأصم: يعني المنافقين أرجأهم الله فلم يخبر عنهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He argues that ‘either’ retains its basic shared sense of one of two possibilities, whether or not it implies doubt in context.
rows.anchor: فهي هنا على أصل موضوعها وهو القدر المشترك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows how their case will end and is wise in what He does with them.
rows.anchor: والله عليم بما يؤول إليه أمرهم، حكيم فيما يفعله بهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Mosque of Harm was built by hypocrites as a meeting place for planning evil, after rival clans envied the Qubāʾ mosque established by ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf.
rows.anchor: ذكر أن منهم من بالغ في الشر حتى ابتنى مجمعا للمنافقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū ʿĀmir the Fāsiq, who fled to Syria after Ḥunayn, urged them to build a mosque near Qubāʾ and promised Roman support to expel Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: وحرضهم أبو عمرو الفاسق على بنائه حين نزل الشام هاربا من وقعة حنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source names twelve alleged builders and says they presented the mosque as a refuge for the sick, needy, and people hindered by rain or cold; Mujammaʿ ibn Jāriya led its prayer.
rows.anchor: وكانوا اثني عشر رجلا من المنافقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mujammaʿ was later regarded as a good Muslim, appointed to lead Qubāʾ by ʿUmar, and sent to Kūfa to teach the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: وهو ممن حسن إسلامه، وولاه عمر إمامة مسجد قباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Tabūk the Prophet stopped at Dhū Awn when the revelation about the mosque came and summoned Mālik ibn al-Dukhshum and the two sons of ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAdī.
rows.anchor: فلما قفل رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من غزوة تبوك نزل بذي أوان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says the Prophet sent men, including ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir and Waḥshī, to demolish and burn the mosque; another says it was demolished without burning.
rows.anchor: ياسر ووحشيا قاتل حمزة بهدمه وتحريقه، فهدم وحرق بنار في سعف

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says they used the mosque for Friday, Saturday, and Sunday prayers before it collapsed on Monday, without being burned.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جريج: صلوا فيه الجمعة والسبت والأحد وانهار يوم الاثنين ولم يحرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Medinan readers and Ibn ʿĀmir read ‘those who’ without conjunction, attested in Medinan and Syrian codices; grammatical options include apposition, a new clause, or an independent subject.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أهل المدينة: نافع، وأبو جعفر، وشيبة، وغيرهم، وابن عامر: الذين بغير واو

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī takes ‘do not stand in it ever’ as the predicate of the preceding subject in the no-wāw reading.
rows.anchor: وقال الكسائي: الخبر لا تقم فيه أبدا

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya proposes supplying an omitted ‘either’ at the beginning or end, with the implied command not to pray in their mosque.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: ويتجه بإضمار إما في أول الآية

rows.speaker: النحاس والحوفي
rows.claim: Al-Naḥḥās and al-Ḥawfī take ‘their building will never cease’ as the predicate.
rows.anchor: وقال النحاس والحوفي: الخبر لا يزال بنيانهم

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawī supplies an omitted predicate such as ‘they are punished.’
rows.anchor: وقال المهدوي: الخبر محذوف تقديره معذبون أو نحوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers add wāw, coordinating the builders with the previously deferred group; it can also begin a new sentence with an independent subject.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جمهور القراء: والذين بالواو عطفا على وآخرون

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī parses ‘those who built’ as accusative specification, though he also allows a subject with an omitted predicate.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: (فإن قلت) : والذين اتخذوا ما محله من الإعراب؟ (قلت) : محله النصب على الاختصاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘For harm’ may be a purpose object meaning opposition to Qubāʾ’s worshippers, strengthening hypocrisy, and dividing believers; it may instead be a circumstantial verbal noun or a second object.
rows.anchor: وانتصب ضرارا على أنه مفعول من أجله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mosque was prepared as a base for Abū ʿĀmir, the man who fought God and His Messenger, to pray in and oppose the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وإرصادا أي: إعدادا لأجل من حارب الله ورسوله وهو أبو عامر الراهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū ʿĀmir died as an exile at Qinnasrīn; the source says this fulfilled his invocation against unbelievers and the Prophet’s invocation against him.
rows.anchor: وكان قد دعا بذلك على الكافرين وأمن الرسول، فكان كما دعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After helping organize the Confederates, Abū ʿĀmir fled from Mecca to Ṭāʾif, then Syria seeking Caesar’s help; he died alone at Qinnasrīn.
rows.anchor: فمات وحيدا طريدا غريبا بقنسرين

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: Kaʿb ibn Mālik’s poem condemns ʿAbd ʿAmr’s treacherous conduct and says he followed faith with unbelief.
rows.anchor: معاذ الله من فعل خبيث ... كسعيك في العشيرة عبد عمرو

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash reads ‘and as an ambush for those who fought God and His Messenger.’
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش: وإرصادا للذين حاربوا الله ورسوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent attachment of ‘before’ is to ‘fought’: Abū ʿĀmir had fought the Prophet before this mosque was built.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن من قبل متعلقا بحارب

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī instead attaches ‘before’ to ‘they built,’ taking it as before the hypocrites’ own hypocrisy; Abū Ḥayyān says this is not apparent.
rows.anchor: وليس بظاهر، والخالف هو بخرج

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains their oath as claiming they sought only the good purpose of prayer, remembrance, and accommodating worshippers.
rows.anchor: ما أردنا ببناء هذا المسجد إلا الخصلة الحسنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān finds al-Zamakhsharī’s two grammatical explanations of ‘we intended only the good’ strained, whether read as an object or as purpose.
rows.anchor: وهذا وجه متكلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet initially considered accompanying them, but revelation came as he called for his shirt to set out.
rows.anchor: فهم الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم بالمشي معهم، واستدعى قميصه لينهض فنزلت

rows.speaker: عيسى بن عمر
rows.claim: ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar reads ‘upon taqwā’ with nunation; Sībawayh records the reading, which later scholars reject, while Ibn Jinnī says the final alif could be an augmentative marker.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عيسى بن عمر على تقوى بالتنوين، وحكى هذه القراءة سيبويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers differ between jرف with a still rāʾ and the majority’s rounded rāʾ; both are dialects, though the rounded form is said to be original.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جماعة منهم: حمزة، وابن عامر، وأبو بكر، جرف بإسكان الراء

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy’s codex adds that the structure’s foundations collapsed with its builder into Hellfire.
rows.anchor: وفي مصحف أبي فانهارت به قواعده في نار جهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators take the passage as contrasting Qubāʾ or the Prophet’s mosque with the Mosque of Harm.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن هذا الكلام فيه تبيين حالي المسجدين

rows.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Jābir says he saw smoke emerging from the Mosque of Harm as it collapsed on Monday.
rows.anchor: وقال جابر بن عبد الله: رأيت الدخان يخرج من مسجد الضرار

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says smoke appeared when the Prophet sent men to demolish the mosque; another report says palm fronds came out burned black and smoke rose from the site.
rows.anchor: وروى سعيد بن جبير: إنه إذ أرسل الرسول بهدمه رؤي منه الدخان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation treats the comparison as a parable: a building founded on Islam and taqwā is better than one founded on shirk and hypocrisy, whose builders fall into Hell.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هذا ضرب مثل أي من أسس بنيانه على الإسلام خير أم من أسس بنيانه على الشرك والنفاق

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya transmits the literal view that the particular mosque itself collapsed into Hell, attributed to Qatāda and Ibn Jurayj.
rows.anchor: قاله: قتادة، وابن جريج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent comparative ‘better’ only makes sense relative to the builder’s own belief that his mosque was good.
rows.anchor: وخير لا شركة بين الأمرين في خير إلا على معتقد باني مسجد الضرار

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī reads the comparison figuratively: true religion rests on firm taqwā, while hypocrisy is a weak precipice; the precipice is not itself a metaphor for everything opposed to piety.
rows.anchor: وضع شفا الجرف في مقابلة التقوى، لا جعل مجازا عن ما ينافي التقوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is linked to the Second, or Greater, ʿAqaba pledge, attended by over seventy Anṣār, including the youngest, ʿUqba ibn ʿAmr.
rows.anchor: نزلت في البيعة الثانية وهي بيعة العقبة الكبرى

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن رواحة
rows.claim: At the pledge, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa asked the Prophet to set the terms for him and for his Lord; the Prophet required protection and commitment to the law and defense of the community.
rows.anchor: والمتكلم بذلك عبد الله بن رواحة، فاشترط صلى الله عليه وسلم حمايته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the Anṣār asked their reward, the Prophet promised Paradise; they accepted, calling it a profitable sale they would neither revoke nor ask to revoke.
rows.anchor: فقالوا: ما لنا على ذلك؟ قال: الجنة، فقالوا: نعم ربح البيع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise applies to everyone in Muḥammad’s community who fights in God’s cause until the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: والآية عامة في كل من جاهد في سبيل الله من أمة محمد

rows.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Jābir reports that a man asked whether the verse had been revealed, heard that it had, declared the sale profitable, and in one version went out to fight and was martyred.
rows.anchor: وعن جابر بن عبد الله: نزلت ورسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم في المسجد

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says every believer on earth has entered into this pledge.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: لا والله إن في الأرض مؤمن إلا وقد أحدث بيعته

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب والأعمش
rows.claim: ʿUmar and al-Aʿmash read ‘and their wealth’ alongside the mention of Paradise.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عمر بن الخطاب والأعمش: وأموالهم بالجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The purchase image portrays reward for giving lives and property; lives come first because they are nobler and cannot be replaced, while ‘purchased’ conveys the buyer’s eagerness and appreciation.
rows.anchor: وقدم الأنفس على الأموال ابتداء بالأشرف وبما لا عوض له إذا فقد

rows.speaker: ابن عيينة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUyayna reads the pledge broadly: believers devote their lives only to obedience and their wealth only to God’s cause, not solely to being killed in battle.
rows.anchor: اشترى منهم أنفسهم أن لا يعملوها إلا في طاعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On Ibn ʿUyayna’s reading, ‘they fight’ begins a new clause describing their highest state; the majority takes it as a circumstantial clause about the fighters.
rows.anchor: وعلى الظاهر وقول الجمهور يكون يقاتلون، في موضع الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readings alternate whether the believers do the killing or are killed; the meaning remains that they fight, with some killing, being killed, both, or neither occurring in different cases.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن، وقتادة، وأبو رجاء، والعربيان، والحرميان، وعاصم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says ‘they fight’ carries an imperative force like the command in 61:11, so it cannot be a circumstantial clause.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: يقاتلون فيه معنى الأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘A promise’ is an emphatic verbal noun restating the promise of Paradise contained in the purchase clause.
rows.anchor: وانتصب وعدا على أنه مصدر مؤكد لمضمون الجملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says God will settle the martyr’s debts owed to other people and compensate them on his behalf.
rows.anchor: روي أنه تعالى يحمل عن الشهيد مظالم العباد ويجازيهم عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the listed virtues are conditions for the fighters’ pledge, making the following verses dependent on the prior purchase; al-Ḍaḥḥāk rebukes a man eager to fight without first meeting the conditions of repentance and worship.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: هذه الصفات شرط في المجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān calls the conditional reading restrictive and burdensome; it drives several competing syntactic analyses of ‘the repentant.’
rows.anchor: وهذا القول فيه حرج وتضييق

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: One parse makes ‘the repentant’ the subject and ‘the worshippers’ its predicate, with each following trait another predicate; al-Zajjāj also allows an omitted predicate meaning they too enter Paradise even without fighting.
rows.anchor: وقيل: خبره محذوف بعد تمام الأوصاف، وتقديره: من أهل الجنة أيضا وإن لم يجاهد قاله الزجاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another parse supplies ‘they are the repentant’ as a detached laudatory phrase, supported by readings that put the following traits in the accusative for praise.
rows.anchor: وقيل: التائبون خبر مبتدأ محذوف تقديره هم التائبون

rows.speaker: الزمخشري وابن عطية
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya allow the listed traits to describe the believers; another possibility makes ‘the repentant’ a substitute for the pronoun in ‘they fight.’
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: ويجوز أن يكون صفة للمؤمنين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās takes ‘the repentant’ as those who turned away from idolatry; al-Ḥasan adds hypocrisy, while another view includes every sin.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: التائبون من الشرك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses ‘worshippers’ as those devoted to prayer or obedient worship; al-Ḥasan says they worship God in both prosperity and hardship.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس: العابدون بالصلاة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وابن عباس وغيرهما
rows.claim: They take ‘wayfarers’ as fasters, likened to travelers who abstain from food and desire; ʿĀʾisha says fasting is this community’s ascetic wandering, and a report attributes this to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: قال ابن مسعود وابن عباس وغيرهما: الصائمون شبهوا بالسائحين في الأرض

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ interprets ‘wayfarers’ as those who fight in God’s cause.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء: السائحون المجاهدون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet recalled an earlier prophet whose people stoned him and who prayed, ‘My Lord, forgive my people, for they do not know.’
rows.anchor: حكى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: عن نبي قبله شجه قومه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because believers might imitate Abraham’s prayer for his father, the passage explains that Abraham withdrew only after his father’s enmity to God became clear.
rows.anchor: بين العلة في استغفار إبراهيم لأبيه، وذكر أنه حين اتضحت له عداوته لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s promise was that he would ask his Lord to forgive his father; Abraham was the speaker, and his father was alive while Abraham hoped he would believe.
rows.anchor: والضمير الفاعل في وعدها عائد على إبراهيم، وكان أبوه بقيد الحياة

rows.speaker: الحسن وآخرون
rows.claim: A group of readers clarifies Abraham as the one promising and his father as the recipient by reading ‘he promised it to his father.’
rows.anchor: قراءة الحسن، وحماد الراوية، وابن السميفع، وأبي نهيك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative makes Abraham’s father promise that he would believe, which sustained Abraham’s hope and prompted his prayer until prohibition came.
rows.anchor: وقيل: لفاعل ضمير والد إبراهيم، وإياه ضمير إبراهيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭalḥa reads the phrase in a past or narrative-present form, ‘Abraham did not ask forgiveness’ or ‘does not ask forgiveness.’
rows.anchor: وقرأ طلحة: وما استغفر إبراهيم، وعنه وما يستغفر إبراهيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says Abraham’s prayer occurred during earthly life, citing his prayers for his father in 26:86 and 14:41; he rejects Ibn Jubayr’s disconnected afterlife scenario of his father becoming a hyena at the bridge.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر أن استغفار إبراهيم لأبيه كان في حالة الدنيا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī asks whether Abraham did not know that asking forgiveness for an unbeliever was forbidden; Abū Ḥayyān says the ban was known through revelation, while reason alone permits God to forgive an unbeliever.
rows.anchor: خفي على إبراهيم عليه السلام أن الاستغفار للكافر غير جائز حتى وعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse reportedly came after someone told the Prophet that he had strayed after his departure, while the speaker followed another way.
rows.anchor: يا رسول الله دنا بعدك بالضلال، إنك على أمر وإنا على غيره فنزلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some believers feared that they had sought forgiveness for polytheists without divine permission; the verse reassures them that God does not count a people astray for an act not previously prohibited.
rows.anchor: وقيل: خاف بعض المؤمنين من الاستغفار للمشركين دون إذن من الله

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says people are not judged for forbidden acts before the prohibition is explained, comparing this with wine drinking and usury before their bans; Abū Ḥayyān sees a Muʿtazilī implication and says rational duties such as truthfulness are not revelation-dependent.
rows.anchor: ولا يؤاخذ به عباده الذين هداهم للإسلام

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid’s gloss is that God would not mislead believers for praying for polytheists before a prohibition was given and explained.
rows.anchor: قال: ما كان ليضلكم بالاستغفار للمشركين بعد إذ هداكم للإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier revelation contexts explain the verse: questions about those who died facing Jerusalem, people who drank wine, and the Bedouin case.
rows.anchor: وتقدم في أسباب النزول ما يشرح به الآية من سؤالهم عمن مات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage continues the rule against praying for polytheists: even the Prophet’s uncle Abū Ṭālib and Abraham’s father could not be forgiven after their unbelief was clear, nor could other unbelieving relatives.
rows.anchor: فمنع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من الاستغفار لعمه أبي طالب

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya defines divine repentance as raising a servant to a higher state, usually from sin to obedience but sometimes from one obedience to a more complete one.
rows.anchor: التوبة من الله رجوعه لعبده من حالة إلى حالة أرفع منه

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Applied here, God raised the Prophet from before enduring the expedition to its completed state; the emigrants and Helpers may have moved from a shortfall to obedience, and the deferred group from disgrace to forgiveness.
rows.anchor: وهذه توبته في هذه الآية على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī connects God’s repentance toward the Prophet with 48:2 and 40:55, urging every believer, even prophets and leading companions, to repent and showing the high status of repentance.
rows.anchor: تاب الله على النبي كقوله تعالى: ليغفر لك الله ما تقدم من ذنبك وما تأخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that God forgave the Prophet for allowing hypocrites to stay behind, as in ‘God forgive you; why did you give them permission?’
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه تاب الله عليه من إذنه للمنافقين في التخلف عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says the emigrants and Helpers had committed faults, but God forgave them for enduring the expedition; mentioning the Prophet with them signals their rank.
rows.anchor: وقيل: لا يبعد أن صدر عن المهاجرين والأنصار أنواع من المخالفات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘They followed him’ may mean they followed his command, by ellipsis, or literally that they set out after the Prophet.
rows.anchor: اتبعوه: أي اتبعوا أمره، فهو من مجاز الحذف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ‘hour of hardship’ is the Tabūk expedition, and may mean the decisive moment of resolve when they accepted its hardship; reward follows that intention even if a poor volunteer later becomes wealthy.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يريد بساعة العسرة الساعة التي وقع فيها عزمهم وانقيادهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the yāʾ reading of ‘their hearts nearly deviate,’ kāda has an impersonal pronoun and ‘hearts’ is raised by the following verb; this avoids treating the delayed subject as the noun of kāda.
rows.anchor: فتعين أن يكون في كاد ضمير الشأن، وارتفاع قلوب بتزيغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the common feminine tāʾ, possible parses make ‘hearts’ the subject of kāda with the predicate between its parts, or make kāda refer to the assembled emigrants and Helpers; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū al-Baqāʾ suggest ‘the people.’
rows.anchor: وقرأ باقي السبعة: بالتاء، فاحتمل أن يكون قلوب اسم كاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each standard parse conflicts with the rule that a near-auxiliary verb’s predicate is an imperfect verb raising a pronoun linked to its subject; interposition also has disputed parallels with kāna.
rows.anchor: وعلى كل واحد من هذه الأعاريب الثلاثة إشكال على ما تقرر في علم النحو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He resolves the grammatical problems by treating kāda as an extra particle with its meaning retained but no syntactic work, supported by Ibn Masʿūd’s reading without it.
rows.anchor: ويخلص من هذه الإشكالات اعتقاد كون كاد زائدة، ومعناها مراد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Kūfans already allow kāda to be extra in 24:40 despite its syntactic effect; that makes it still more plausible here where it does no grammatical work.
rows.anchor: وقد ذهب الكوفيون إلى زيادتها في قوله تعالى: لم يكد يراها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash and al-Jaḥdarī read the verb with a raised tāʾ; Ubayy adds a feminine ending to kāda. The repeated ‘then He turned toward them’ refers to the earlier believers or the group and emphasizes the point.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش والجحدري: تزيغ برفع التاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating ‘then He turned toward them’ may emphasize acceptance, distinguish initiating repentance from sustaining it, or ensure that those whose hearts nearly deviated are explicitly included; God’s compassion is the reason for His acceptance.
rows.anchor: أو لأنه لما ذكر أن فريقا منهم كادت قلوبهم تزيغ نص على التوبة ثانيا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the three were left behind from the Tabūk expedition.
rows.anchor: ومعنى خلفوا عن الغزو غزو تبوك قاله: قتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says they were left pending after Abū Lubāba’s group was forgiven; their case was delayed fifty days before their repentance was accepted.
rows.anchor: حيث تيب عليهم بعد التوبة على أبي لبابة وأصحابه إرجاء أمرهم خمسين يوما

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: Kaʿb ibn Mālik himself rejected the physical-delay interpretation: they were left without acceptance of their excuses, not simply left behind on the expedition.
rows.anchor: وقد رد تأويل قتادة كعب بن مالك بنفسه فقال: معنى خلفوا تركوا عن قبول العذر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers vary between passive ‘they were left behind’ forms, active ‘they left behind the fighters’ or ‘became corrupt,’ and ‘they differed’ with an added alif; al-Bāqir says the passive gloss would not fit.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو زيد، وأبو مجلز، والشعبي، وابن يعمر، وعلي بن الحسين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash’s ‘the three left behind’ is likely an explanatory reading because it differs from the consonantal codex text.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش: وعلى الثلاثة المخلفين، ولعله قرأ كذلك على سبيل التفسير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The constriction of the earth is a figure for isolation; the constriction of their selves depicts grief and anxiety filling them so fully that no comfort or joy could enter.
rows.anchor: وضاقت عليهم أنفسهم استعارة، لأن الهم والغم ملأها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī reads ‘they thought’ as ‘they knew’; Ibn ʿAṭiyya glosses it as certainty, while another view keeps ordinary conjecture because the duration of their hardship remained uncertain.
rows.anchor: وظنوا أي: علموا. قاله الزمخشري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s sequence moves from social alienation, to inward distress, and finally to despair of human help and complete turning to God alone.
rows.anchor: فذكر أولا ضيق الأرض عليهم وهو كناية عن استيحاشهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects treating thumma as extra or making the clause after it the conditional answer, since Arabic usage does not support an extra thumma.
rows.anchor: ودعوى أن ثم زائدة وجواب إذا ما بعد ثم بعيد جدا، وغير ثابت من لسان العرب زيادة ثم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others take ‘when’ after ‘until’ as a temporal endpoint without conditional force: they were left until that time, then God again accepted them and showed mercy.
rows.anchor: ومن زعم أن إذا بعد حتى قد تجرد من الشرط وتبقى لمجرد الوقت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘So that they repent’ can mean staying firm in repentance and not undoing it, or returning to their usual social intercourse with believers and regaining calm.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معنى ليتوبوا ليدوموا على التوبة ولا يراجعوا ما يبطلها

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the verse begins with God’s action when recounting a divine favor, but begins with the sinner when describing blame, as in 16:100.
rows.anchor: بدأ في ترتيبه بالجهة التي هي عن الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The full account of the three is in al-Bukhārī and Muslim’s expedition reports, so the commentator abbreviates it.
rows.anchor: وقد خرج حديثهم بكماله البخاري ومسلم وهو في السير، فلذلك اختصرت سوقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their offense merited severity because leaders and exemplars bear greater responsibility; Kaʿb was an ʿAqaba veteran and his companions were veterans of Badr, unlike ordinary men.
rows.anchor: إذ هو أسوة وحجة للمنافقين والطاعنين، إذ كان كعب من أهل العقبة

rows.speaker: الأوزاعي
rows.claim: Al-Awzāʿī’s letter to Caliph al-Manṣūr says kinship with the Prophet only increases one’s duty to God and the public’s right to object when one disobeys.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن قرابتك من رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لن تزيد حق الله عليك إلا عظما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The obligation to accompany the Prophet applied when the Muslim community was small and was later superseded by 9:122; if an enemy attacks a region, however, fighting becomes individually obligatory there.
rows.anchor: ثم نسخ عند قوة الإسلام بقوله: وما كان المؤمنون لينفروا كافة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reward language explains the duty to go out and risk oneself: believers endure hardship and thereby hurt Islam’s enemies.
rows.anchor: ذلك الوجوب للخروج وبذل النفس هو بسبب ما أعد الله لهم من الثواب الجسيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thirst means thirst; a lengthened variant is reported. The order lists thirst, fatigue, then hunger because travel in Tabūk’s heat made thirst and exhaustion acute, while hunger can be endured longer.
rows.anchor: والظمأ العطش

rows.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
rows.claim: ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr reads ẓamāʾ with a long vowel, analogous to the noun safāh.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبيد بن عمير ظماء بالمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘A place trodden’ may denote either a place or the act of treading; what angers unbelievers includes travel through their lands or Muslim lands, and treading includes hooves and feet.
rows.anchor: وموطئا مفعل من وطئ، فاحتمل أن يكون مكانا، واحتمل مصدرا

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn ʿAlī reads ‘causes anger’ with a ḍamma on the yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي: يغيظ بضم الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘A gain or injury’ can mean the act of gaining or its object, and is broad enough to include small or great losses to enemies, including killing, capture, spoil, or defeat; it is not a form of the root for giving.
rows.anchor: والنيل مصدر، فاحتمل أن يبقى على موضوعه، واحتمل أن يراد به المنيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording generalizes enemies through the definite plural and through the indefinite ‘any enemy’ in a negative context; it first names hardships to the travelers, then effects on the enemy.
rows.anchor: جاء العموم في الكفار بالألف واللام، وفي من عدو لكونه في سياق النفي

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī allows ‘treading’ to mean striking or destroying, not merely walking, citing a Prophetic report about God’s last attack at Wajj.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يراد بالوطء الإيقاع والإبادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘It is written’ may refer literally to entries in records or the Preserved Tablet, or figuratively to a deed being firmly established for reward.
rows.anchor: والكتب هنا يحتمل أن يكون حقيقة أي: كتب في الصحائف، أو في اللوح المحفوظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause ‘it is written for them’ is circumstantial; its singular pronoun can treat the preceding verbal action as a demonstrative-like collective, or refer to the mentioned good deed.
rows.anchor: والجملة من كتب في موضع الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report promises protection from Hell for feet dustied in God’s cause; Ibn ʿAbbās says every fear suffered earns seventy thousand good deeds.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: بكل روعة تنالهم في سبيل الله سبعون ألف حسنة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās defines a small expense as a date or similar amount; al-Zamakhsharī adds even a whip’s thong, and calls ʿUthmān’s Army of Hardship expenditure a large one.
rows.anchor: والنفقة الصغيرة قال ابن عباس: كالتمرة ونحوها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The small expense is named before the large to stress that even the least is recorded; a fortiori, the greater is rewarded.
rows.anchor: وقدم صغيرة على سبيل الاهتمام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object of ‘it is written’ may be the action implied by spending and crossing ground, or the previously mentioned ‘good deed.’
rows.anchor: ومفعول كتب مضمر يعود على المصدر المفهوم من ينفقون ويقطعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earlier clauses describe harder burdens and greater harm to enemies; spending and travel are easier and rewarded whether or not they produce those effects. The nominal clause with ‘indeed’ reinforces the former promise, and ‘the doers of good’ marks their rank.
rows.anchor: وتأخرت هاتان الجملتان وقدمت تلك الجمل السابقة لأنها أشق على النفس

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī’s first interpretation makes ‘best’ describe their deeds, which include obligatory and recommended acts but not merely permissible ones; the best acts may stand as an inclusive substitute for them.
rows.anchor: الأول: أن أحسن من صفة فعلهم، وفيها الواجب والمندوب دون المباح

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī offers two readings of ‘to reward them according to the best of what they did’: either God rewards their deeds with their best or chosen reward, or ‘best’ describes the reward as superior to their works.
rows.anchor: والثاني: أن الأحسن صفة للجزاء أي: يجزيهم جزاء هو أحسن من أعمالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān questions the second reading: if ‘best’ describes reward, it is unclear why that reward is annexed to the deeds or how the comparison is formed.
rows.anchor: فكيف أضيف إلى الأعمال وليس بعضها منها؟ وكيف يقع التفضيل إذ ذاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following the warning that people’s transgression harms themselves, the parable reminds them how quickly worldly life disappears after it delights them.
rows.anchor: ضرب مثلا عجيبا غريبا للحياة الدنيا تذكر من يبغي فيها على سرعة زوالها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī calls this a compound simile: the world’s rapid decline after its flourishing resembles lush vegetation becoming dry debris.
rows.anchor: هذا من التشبيه المركب، شبهت حال الدنيا في سرعة تقضيها وانقراض نعيمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Only’ is not restrictive here, in either lexical meaning or usage, because the Qur’an gives other parables for worldly life.
rows.anchor: وإنما هنا ليست للحصر لا وضعا ولا استعمالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Parable’ may mean a description or a proverbial comparison; the apparent image compares worldly life with water in what it enables and how its benefit ends.
rows.anchor: والمثل هنا يحتمل أن يراد به الصفة، وأن يراد به القول السائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other parses compare worldly life to vegetation nourished by water, with a deleted noun, or to people’s life renewed by rain; the phrase about its owners thinking they can control it supports the latter.
rows.anchor: وقيل: شبهت الحياة الدنيا بالنبات على تلك الأوصاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘The sky’ may refer to clouds or to the direction of the sky; the apparent reading is that vegetation mingled with rain by clinging to and taking it as nourishment.
rows.anchor: والسماء إما أن يراد من السحاب، وإما أن يراد من جهة السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ can indicate accompaniment: each of two things can be said to mix with the other, and the rain nourishes every part of the plant.
rows.anchor: وكل مختلطين يصح في كل منهما أن يقال: اختلط بصاحبه

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmānī takes the mixing as adjacency, since mixture ordinarily involves interpenetration; Abū Ḥayyān says interpenetration itself is possible and need not be reduced to adjacency.
rows.anchor: وقال الكرماني: فاختلط به اختلاط مجاورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He considers ‘varied,’ ‘composed,’ and ‘extended’ possible suggested senses of the verb, but says the wording does not support ‘varied.’
rows.anchor: وقيل: اختلط اختلف وتنوع بالماء، وينبو لفظ اختلط عن هذا التفسير
